# Jacek Karpiński
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a pioneering Polish computer engineer whose career was marked by significant technical achievements and formidable challenges. Born into a family of intellectuals and alpinists, he joined the resistance during World War II, surviving serious injuries and participating in the Warsaw Uprising. After the war, he quickly distinguished himself academically and professionally: he built early electronic devices such as the AAH (1957), constructed Poland's (and arguably the world's) first transistor-based differential equation analyzer (AKAT-1, 1959), and created one of the first perceptrons outside the US (1964). His most notable work was the K-202 minicomputer (early 1970s), which was innovative with its use of microchips, asynchronous architecture, memory segmentation with paging, and rapid computational capabilities. However, due to political obstacles, internal opposition, and lack of state support, only a handful were produced.
Karpiński faced persistent setbacks, including censorship, bureaucratic interference, political feuds, and eventual marginalization from Poland’s computer industry. Despite offers to emigrate, he remained in Poland until late in life, working on various inventions and later serving briefly as a consultant. He was also a controversial figure due to his wartime and postwar intelligence cooperation, with debates over the magnitude and suppression of his engineering contributions. He received national honors late in life and his legacy is now recognized in Polish technological history and popular culture.
